query: Consider the following context: High entropy alloy nanoparticles bring hope to developing more efficient nanomaterials for high‐temperature applications. Nevertheless, the enhanced thermal stability of nearly equiatomic nanoalloys containing at least 5 metals is nothing more than theoretical speculation about the impact of thermodynamic contributions on their structural properties and remains to be proven. In that context, which method can be used for investigate at the atomic scale the thermal behavior of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Using in situ high‐resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) with an integrated heating stage will enable atomic‐scale investigation of the thermal behavior of AuCoCuNiPt high‐entropy nanoparticles by directly observing temperature‐induced atomic rearrangements and phase transformations.
generation.material_initial_state: Nearly equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles exhibiting a disordered solid‐solution structure at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Application of controlled in situ heating within an aberration‐corrected TEM setup.
generation.conditions: Under high vacuum (or inert gas) conditions with a precisely calibrated heating stage to incrementally raise the nanoparticle temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Atomic lattice distortions and phase transitions that mediate changes in local order as thermal energy is introduced.
generation.mechanism: As the nanoparticles are heated, thermal energy overcomes diffusion barriers leading to atomic rearrangements that may manifest as phase transitions or ordering phenomena. This real‐time observation links the thermodynamic driving forces (e.g., high configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion) to the structural stability at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Real‐time, atomic‐scale imaging will reveal temperature-induced atomic rearrangements (e.g., local ordering or phase transformation) that correlate with enhanced thermal stability compared to predictions based solely on thermodynamic contributions.
generation.baseline: The room temperature structure, characterized by a disordered high-entropy configuration with no visible phase transitions under static conditions.
generation.boundary: Limitations might include beam-induced effects under TEM irradiation and potential inability to reach extremely high temperatures without compromising image resolution.
generation.uncertainty: The specific temperature at which measurable atomic rearrangements or phase transitions occur may vary and require further calibration; additionally, distinguishing intrinsic thermal effects from beam artifacts remains challenging.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles and place them in an aberration‐corrected TEM equipped with an in situ heating stage. Incrementally increase the temperature while continuously imaging the atomic lattice. Record diffraction patterns and high-resolution images to capture any onset of order or phase change.
measurements: High-resolution TEM images at each temperature step
In situ selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns
Temperature calibration to correlate structural changes with thermal input
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant atomic rearrangements, changes in diffraction patterns, or phase transformations are observed at elevated temperatures—even after surpassing expected thermal activation thresholds—then the hypothesis that in situ HRTEM can resolve the thermally induced atomic-scale behavior in these nanoparticles would be falsified.

Alloy ingots with a nominal composition of Al x CoCrFeNi ( x = 0.1, 0.75 and 1.5) were synthesized by arc-melting a mixture of pure metals (purity >99.6 wt.%) in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere. These ingots were remelted at least four times to ensure chemical homogeneity. Melted alloys were eventually drop-cast into a mold Φ 5 × 70 mm 3 . The solidified ingots were cut into thin pieces 1 mm thick and one side polished. The sample densities for x = 0.1, 0.75 and 1.5, which were measured by Archimedes method, are 8.1, 7.4 and 6.9 g·cm −3 , respectively. The microstructures of as-prepared Al x CoCrFeNi HEAs ( x = 0.1, 0.75 and 1.5) are single fcc, fcc plus ordered bcc (B2) and B2 plus disordered bcc (A2), respectively. The XRD and SEM characterization results are given in Supplementary Figs S2 and S3 , the detailed microstructure characterizations can be also found in our previous study [14] .
